I. THE MYSTERIOUS MUSHROOMS

Pipkin the field mouse was in a great hurry. He always was. He prided himself on being the swiftest creature in the meadow, and he scurried from clover to dandelion with a flick of his tail and a twitch of his nose. "Nobody can catch me!" he would often squeak to anyone who would listen. "Not even the shadow of the hawk!"

One morning, he came upon a strange sight near the old stone wall. A cluster of new mushrooms had appeared overnight. But they were not like any mushrooms he had ever seen. They were a brilliant, waxy red with perfect white spots, and they stood in a neat, proud little circle.

"Goodness!" Pipkin whispered to himself. He crept closer, his whiskers trembling with curiosity.

Just then, a slow, rustling sound came from the tall grass. It was Bartholomew, the old garden snake, sunning himself on a warm patch of earth. "I would not go so near if I were you, little one," Bartholomew hissed softly. His voice was dry and whispery, like leaves skittering across the ground.

"And why not?" Pipkin demanded, puffing out his chest. "They are only mushrooms. I am not afraid of a fungus! I shall run right through the middle of them!"

"Ah!" said Bartholomew, not moving an inch. "But some things that are beautiful are not meant to be touched. My grandmother once told me that such mushrooms are painted by the fairies. They are for looking at only."

Pipkin let out a tiny, scornful laugh. "Fairies! What nonsense! You are slow and cautious, Bartholomew. I am quick and clever. I will be in and out before these 'fairy mushrooms' even know I am there!" And before the old snake could offer another word of warning, Pipkin took a deep breath, crouched down, and shot forward like a little brown arrow.

He darted straight into the center of the circle. And then he stopped. A strange, sticky feeling was on his paws. He tried to lift his right foot, but it would not come up. He tried to lift his left, and it, too, was stuck fast. The beautiful red mushrooms were not mushrooms at all! They were little wooden knobs, painted brightly and coated with the thick, gooey sap that Gardener John used to fix his tool handles.

"Help!" Pipkin squealed, his voice trembling with fright. "I am trapped! I cannot move!"

Bartholomew sighed a long, slow sigh and began to slither towards him. "Patience, little mouse," he said calmly. "Speed is a fine thing; but it is not the only thing. It seems you have run into trouble faster than you can run out of it."

II. A STICKY SITUATION

Gardener John had set the painted knobs in a circle and coated them with tree sap, hoping to discover what creature had been nibbling his prize-winning carrots. He had not expected to catch a foolish little field mouse.

Pipkin struggled and squirmed, but his frantic efforts only mired him deeper in the sticky trap. His fine fur was becoming matted with sap, and tears of panic welled in his tiny black eyes. "Oh, what shall I do?" he cried. "I shall be stuck here forever!"

"Stop your wiggling," Bartholomew commanded, his voice sharp but not unkind. "You will only make it worse. Be still now, and let me think." The old snake circled the trap slowly, his forked tongue flicking out to taste the air. He examined the situation from every angle. "This is a very sticky problem," he mused. "But there is a solution to most problems, if one is clever enough to find it."

"But you said I was the clever one!" Pipkin wailed. "And look at me now!"

"You are quick, not clever," Bartholomew corrected him gently. "Cleverness takes time. Now, I have an idea. There is a pile of dry dust by the potato patch where the sparrows like to bathe. If I can bring enough of it here, it may coat the sap and make it less sticky. It will be a slow job."

"Oh, please try!" begged Pipkin. "I will be patient! I promise I will never boast about my speed again!"

So Bartholomew began his work. He slithered to the dusty patch, rolled his long body in the fine, powdery earth until he was coated in it, and returned to the trap. He rubbed his sides against the sap around Pipkin's feet, leaving a layer of dust behind. The sap became less tacky. Over and over again he made the trip; back and forth, from the dust patch to the trap. It was slow, tiring work.

At last, after what seemed like an age to the anxious mouse, Bartholomew said, "Now, try to pull. But do it slowly."

Pipkin gave a gentle, steady tug. One foot came free! Then another! Soon he was standing on the grass outside the circle, sticky and dirty and ashamed, but free.

"Oh, thank you, Bartholomew!" he chattered. "You saved me! How can I ever repay you?"

The old snake coiled himself into a comfortable loop. "You can repay me by remembering this," he said. "Sometimes the slowest path is the safest one. And it is always wise to listen to those who have seen more seasons than you." Pipkin nodded his head vigorously. He was still the swiftest creature in the meadow; but he had learned that there were some things more important than being fast.

The mare seemed to have no answer for that. She merely flattened her ears for a moment before turning her attention back to the blacksmith.

Ebenezer looked at Twinkleheels. "Pay her no mind," he said in a low voice. "Some horses mistake a sharp tongue for a sharp wit. Her shoes do not make her wise."

Twinkleheels felt a little better. He watched as the blacksmith, a large, cheerful man named Mr. Gable with arms as thick as fence posts and a smudged, kindly face, finished his work. With a final tap-tap-tap of his hammer, he straightened up and patted the white mare's flank.

"There you are, Daisy," he boomed. "Good as new, and ready for the icy roads."

A man who had been waiting by the door came forward, paid Mr. Gable a few coins, and led the white mare away. As she passed, she gave Twinkleheels one last scornful look. But this time Twinkleheels did not feel angry. He felt only a little sorry for her. It must be unpleasant to be so sour.

"Well now, Farmer Green," the blacksmith said, wiping his hands on his heavy leather apron. "It is good to see you. And old Ebenezer, too! What can I do for this fine gentleman today?"

"He cast a shoe in the woodlot yesterday, Mr. Gable," Farmer Green replied. "And I thought the other three looked about ready to go. And this little fellow," he added, laying a warm hand on Twinkleheels' neck, "is ready for his very first set."

Mr. Gable's eyes twinkled. "His first set! Well, that is a special day. A very special day indeed. We will make him a fine set of shoes he can be proud of. But we will let the older gentleman go first. He knows the ropes."

Mr. Gable untied Ebenezer and led him to the middle of the wide, earthen floor. Twinkleheels watched, his earlier nervousness returning like a winter chill. He was glad that Ebenezer was going first. He could see exactly what was going to happen.

"Alright, old friend," the smith said gently. "Let's see that foot."

Without any fuss at all, Ebenezer lifted his left front hoof and rested it on the low stool the smith put before him. He stood perfectly still on his three remaining legs, as if he were merely resting in his own stall.

First, Mr. Gable took a pair of pincers and with a few skillful twists, he pulled out the old, bent nails from the hoof wall. Then the old, worn shoe came off with a dull clink. He tossed it onto a glittering pile of old iron in the corner. Then he picked up a tool that looked like a very coarse file. It made a loud, rasping sound as he drew it across the bottom of Ebenezer's hoof, trimming and smoothing the horny edge.

Twinkleheels shifted his weight from one foot to another. The sound was unpleasant, and he could not imagine it felt very good. But Ebenezer did not even twitch an ear.

When the hoof was neat and tidy, Mr. Gable took a piece of string and made a careful measurement. Then he walked over to a rack of new horseshoes. He selected one, squinted at it, and shook his head. He carried it over to the fiery forge. With a long pair of tongs, he thrust the iron shoe deep into the glowing coals. Then he began to pump a great handle on the side of the forge, and the fire roared to life with a mighty WHOOSH, turning from red to a brilliant, sun-bright yellow.

In a moment, he pulled the horseshoe out. It glowed a fiery cherry red, and heat shimmered in the air all around it. He laid it on the anvil, and then the terrible clanging began again.

CLANG! CLANG! CLANG!

Mr. Gable's hammer rose and fell, striking the glowing metal with a powerful rhythm. Sparks flew in every direction like angry fireflies. Twinkleheels wanted to bolt for the door, but he saw that Johnnie Green was standing right beside him, and that old Ebenezer had not moved a muscle. So he stood his ground, though his heart was beating like a drum.

Then came the part that frightened him most of all. The smith carried the still-glowing shoe over to Ebenezer. Twinkleheels held his breath. He was sure it would burn him terribly. Mr. Gable pressed the hot shoe against Ebenezer's hoof for just a second. A little puff of white smoke rose up, and a strange, sharp smell filled the air. It was the smell of burning hoof.

Twinkleheels gave a little gasp of fright. But Ebenezer turned his head and spoke to him, his voice as quiet and untroubled as ever.

"That does not hurt, little one," he said. "The hoof has no feeling on the bottom, just as your hair has no feeling when it is cut. The smith does this to make a perfect fit. See? It is all done."

And it was. Mr. Gable took the shoe to the tub of water, and with a final, loud HISS, he plunged it in. A great cloud of steam rose to the rafters. When he pulled it out, the shoe was black and cool.

He placed it against Ebenezer's hoof again, and this time it fit perfectly. Then, taking a few small, special nails from his apron, he held the shoe in place and began to hammer.

Tap. Tap. Tap.

Each blow was quick and certain. He drove the nails through the holes in the shoe and up through the side of the hoof wall, where there was no feeling. Then with a twist of his tools, he clipped the sharp ends of the nails off and smoothed them down.

One shoe was on! Ebenezer put his foot down, and it rested firmly on the ground. The smith repeated the process for the horse's other three feet, working with a calm speed that Twinkleheels found amazing. In what seemed like a very short time, Ebenezer was shod all around with a fine new set of shoes.

"Now for the young fellow!" Mr. Gable said, his smile seeming to light up the dim corners of the shop. He came toward Twinkleheels.

Twinkleheels' bravery suddenly vanished. He backed up a step, pulling on his halter rope.

Johnnie Green came at once to his head and began stroking his nose. "It's alright, Twinkleheels," he whispered. "You saw Ebenezer. It doesn't hurt a bit. You must be brave now."

"He's a little timid," Farmer Green said to the smith. "He's never seen the inside of a place like this before."

"And that is perfectly natural," said Mr. Gable in his kind, booming voice. "There's a lot of noise and fire in here. Enough to startle anyone. But we will be gentle with him." He approached slowly and held out the back of his hand for Twinkleheels to sniff. It smelled of metal and smoke and horses.

"Come now," the smith said. "Let's have a look at those little feet. Which one shall we give a shoe to first?"

Twinkleheels did not know what to do. He remembered what he had told Ebenezer, about not knowing which foot to hold up first. He looked at Ebenezer, who was now tied to a ring on the far wall, watching him. The old horse gave a slight nod, as if to say, "You can do it."

Twinkleheels took a deep breath. He would obey orders, just as Ebenezer had told him to.

The blacksmith chuckled. "We'll start with the left front, how about that?" He ran his hand down Twinkleheels' leg and then gently but firmly tapped his fetlock. "Up now, little one."

Hesitantly, Twinkleheels lifted his foot. The smith caught it and rested it on his leather-covered knee. It felt very strange to have his foot held by a man. He wanted to snatch it away, but Johnnie's steadying hand on his neck gave him courage.

Then the rasping began. RASP! RASP! It was a dreadfully loud noise so close to his own leg, and it tickled! He wiggled and tried to pull his foot back.

"Whoa there! Steady, boy," Farmer Green said from his other side.

"Just making them neat and level for your new shoes," Mr. Gable explained in a calm, rumbling voice. "You can't put a new shoe on a ragged hoof."

Twinkleheels forced himself to be still. It did not hurt. It was just strange and ticklish. Soon the smith was done filing. He took another measurement with his string.

"Well now!" he declared. "These will be the smallest shoes I've made all winter! Fit for a pony prince!"

Twinkleheels felt a little swell of pride. A pony prince! He watched as Mr. Gable went through the whole process again: the roaring forge, the glowing red horseshoe, the loud clanging on the anvil. The sounds were still startling, but they were no longer so frightening, for now he understood them. They were the sounds of his new shoes being made.

Then came the moment he had been dreading. Mr. Gable came towards him with the hot, glowing shoe in his tongs. Twinkleheels trembled. He shut his eyes tight. He smelled the sharp, smoky scent of his own hoof as the shoe was pressed against it for a bare instant. He flinched hard and gave a little snort of alarm.

"Whoa, son! Easy now!" said Farmer Green, his hand firm on his shoulder.

"It's alright, it's alright," the smith said in a low, soothing voice. "Just for a second. See? All done. You did not even feel it."

Twinkleheels opened his eyes. It was true. He had felt the heat near his leg, but there had been no pain at all. Not a bit! Ebenezer had been right all along.

The blacksmith cooled the little shoe with a sizzle and a hiss, and then he brought it back. He held it in place and picked up his hammer and a nail.

"Now for the tapping," he said. "You're a brave fellow."

Tap. Tap. Tap. Twinkleheels held his breath. He could feel the small vibrations traveling up his leg, but there was no pain. It was a funny, dull feeling, nothing more. In a moment, the first shoe was securely nailed to his hoof.

Mr. Gable gently placed his foot back on the ground. It felt different. It felt heavier.

"There now," the smith said. "One down, three to go. You see? Nothing to it."

And Twinkleheels found that he was right. The second foot was much easier. He still flinched a little at the smell of the hot shoe, but he knew it would not hurt him. By the time Mr. Gable started on his hind feet, Twinkleheels was standing almost as still as Ebenezer had. He felt very grown-up and sensible. He was paying attention and obeying orders, and he was not having any trouble.

At last, all four shoes were on.

"There you go, little pony," Mr. Gable said, giving him a final, friendly pat on the rump. "You're ready for the stoniest roads and the iciest paths now. You stood like a champion for your first shoeing. A real champion!"

Twinkleheels felt as if he might burst with pride. A champion! Johnnie Green untied his rope.

"Let's see you walk, boy," he said, and he led Twinkleheels in a small circle on the hard floor of the smithy.

Click, clack, click, clack.

It was a wonderful, new sound! His very own sound! It was crisp and loud and important. He lifted his feet higher than usual, just to hear the delightful noise he made. He stretched out his neck and looked down, trying to see the small, dark crescents of iron that were now a part of him.

Ebenezer watched him from across the shop. "They suit you well," the old horse said, and Twinkleheels thought he saw the hint of a smile on his friend's face. "Now you are a proper working pony."

Farmer Green paid Mr. Gable, thanking him for his patience and skill. Then he untied Ebenezer. "Time to go home, gentleman," he said.

Johnnie led Twinkleheels out into the bright, cold air. Ebenezer was already being hitched to the buggy. Twinkleheels took his place behind it, his head held very high.

As they started off, they came to a part of the road where the wind had swept the snow clean, leaving a patch of frozen, bare ground. Twinkleheels' new shoes rang against it with a clear, musical rhythm.

Clip-clop, clip-clop, clip-clop!

It was the most grown-up sound he had ever made. It was the sound a real horse made, a horse with important work to do.

"Listen, Ebenezer!" he called out, trotting proudly. "Listen to me! I sound just like you now!"

Ebenezer's great head turned slightly. "You do indeed," he answered, his voice full of amusement. "It is a fine sound. But mind you do not get so busy listening to your feet that you trip over them."

Twinkleheels did not mind the gentle warning. He was too happy. He trotted all the way home, listening to his new music on every bare patch of road.

When they arrived back at the farm, old dog Spot ran out, barking a happy welcome. He stopped and cocked his head as Twinkleheels clattered into the yard, as if he were hearing a new horse entirely.

Johnnie led Twinkleheels into the long, quiet barn. The two bay horses, who were often so quick to laugh at him, were in their stalls. They looked over as Twinkleheels walked down the central aisle. His new shoes made a loud, confident clatter on the wooden floorboards, a sound much louder than the soft patter he used to make.

"Well, listen to him!" said one of the bays, whose name was Rusty. "What's all that noise?"

"He sounds like he is wearing pots on his feet," said the other, whose name was Dusty.

But Twinkleheels did not care what they said. He stopped right in front of their stalls and held his head as high as it would go. "I have been to the smithy," he announced in a clear voice. "I have been shod." And to prove it, he lifted his left front foot and showed them the neat, dark iron shoe fastened there.

Rusty and Dusty fell silent. They peered at the shoe, and then at Twinkleheels' other feet. They had shoes, of course, but they had worn them for so long they could not remember their own first time at the blacksmith's shop. For once, they had nothing to laugh at. In fact, they looked just a little bit impressed.

Johnnie put Twinkleheels back in his stall next to Ebenezer and gave him a fresh helping of sweet hay and a loving pat. Twinkleheels felt tired from his exciting day, but he was very, very pleased with himself. He was no longer just a pasture pony. He was a pony with shoes. He was Twinkleheels, the champion.

He took a mouthful of hay and began to chew, thinking over the events of the day.

"Thank you, Ebenezer," he said quietly to the old horse in the next stall. "Thank you for coming with me today. I was very frightened."

Ebenezer turned his head. "You had a right to be," he replied kindly. "The smithy is a frightening place at first. But you were very brave."

"I did not feel brave," Twinkleheels confessed. "I felt like running away."

"Ah," said Ebenezer, his voice low and wise. "But you see, little one, that is what bravery is. Bravery is not being unafraid. It is being afraid, and standing still to do what you must do anyway."

Twinkleheels thought about this for a long time. He thought about the roaring fire, the terrible clanging, and the strange, sharp smells. He had been afraid of all those things. But he had stood still. He had let Mr. Gable give him his shoes.

He decided that Ebenezer was right. And he decided that he liked being brave even more than he liked being fast. With that happy and important thought, he put his head down in his hay and felt the strange, solid, and satisfying weight of his wonderful new shoes.

"You are quite right, ma'am," he said, his voice quiet and steady. "I was foolish and went where I should not have gone. I have a lot to learn."

Flash snorted, a loud, dismissive sound. "I don't get stuck!" he declared. "I'm too fast! I'd fly right over a snowdrift. You're just slow, that's your trouble." He turned his attention back to his own reflection in a bucket of water, admiring the toss of his mane.

Ebenezer watched the exchange with a thoughtful expression. Mr. Hammerhand just shook his head and chuckled to himself.

Soon, Twinkleheels had four shining shoes on his feet once more. He tested his left front foot. It felt solid. Balanced. Strong. But this time, the feeling of strength was different. It was not a giddy, boastful pride. It was a quiet, steady confidence. He knew what the shoes were for, and he knew what they were not for.

"Thank you, Mr. Hammerhand," he neighed softly as Johnnie led him out into the bright, cold air.

On the journey home, Twinkleheels trotted along behind Ebenezer, his new shoe making a crisp, ringing sound on the packed snow. He felt good. He felt whole again.

"That colt, Flash," he said after a while, "he reminded me of myself."

"Did he now?" Ebenezer asked, his ears twitching back to listen.

"Yes," Twinkleheels admitted. "He thinks being fast is the only thing that matters. I think he will have to learn a hard lesson soon."

"Perhaps he will," said Ebenezer. "Some lessons must be learned the hard way. There is no telling them. You were lucky, little one. You had your father, Farmer Green, to dig you out. And you had Bright and Broad to clear the path. That young colt may not be so fortunate."

Twinkleheels thought about the two great, gentle oxen. He thought of their slow, steady strength that had saved him. He had been so impatient with them before. Now, he felt nothing but gratitude.

When they arrived back at the farm, old dog Spot ran out to greet them, his tail wagging furiously. "You're all fixed!" he barked happily. "Four shoes again!"

The two bay horses, Lightfoot and High-step, were in the paddock, kicking up their heels. They trotted over to the fence as Johnnie led Twinkleheels toward the barn.

"Well, look who it is," Lightfoot called out. "I heard you lost something shiny yesterday, Twinkleheels."

"Did you go back to find it in the snow?" High-step added with a mocking whinny.

A day ago, their teasing would have stung him. He would have felt ashamed, or would have tried to think of a clever reply. But now, he simply stopped and looked at them calmly.

"Yes, I did lose it," he answered, his voice even. "And I went back and got a new one. I found a little bit of sense along the way, too. It's much more useful than a horseshoe."

Lightfoot and High-step just stared at him. They did not seem to know what to say to that. Johnnie Green, who had heard, grinned and gave Twinkleheels an extra firm pat on the neck. "That's telling them, Twink," he whispered.

Inside the warm, familiar-smelling barn, Farmer Green unhitched Ebenezer while Johnnie led Twinkleheels to his stall. Across the aisle, Bright and Broad were munching their afternoon hay. They lifted their great heads as Twinkleheels came in, their dark eyes placid and patient.

Twinkleheels looked at them, and for the first time, he did not feel small or impatient or jealous. He felt a deep, warm respect. He gave a low, friendly whicker in their direction. One of them, Broad, flicked an ear in acknowledgment before returning to his meal.

It was a small gesture, but to Twinkleheels it felt like a welcome. He was not an ox. He could not break paths through shoulder-high drifts. But he was a pony, with four good shoes and quick feet for the clear roads. And he was part of the same farm. He belonged.

It was enough, he decided, to be good at the things you were meant to do. It was more than enough.

With a quiet, humble sigh of contentment, Twinkleheels put his head down to his own sweet hay and began to eat. He was still Twinkleheels, but he was a little older now, and a great deal wiser. And he was happy.

Starlight let out a huff of contempt. "Nonsense! A little mud never hurt anyone. He's a coward, that's all. A timid little pony who is afraid to lose."

"He is not!" Johnnie's face was red with anger. "He beat Ebenezer in a race once! And Ebenezer is very wise!"

"He beat that old relic?" Starlight laughed again. "That proves nothing. I could beat him while trotting backwards. Very well, if the pony is too scared to race, we shall simply go for a ride. But do try to keep up, won't you?"

"The pony's right, boys," he said calmly. "The ground is treacherous today. It's slippery and soft. No day for racing. You just have a nice, slow ride, and be careful when you get to the creek. The banks will be slick as glass."

Fred looked annoyed, but he said nothing to his uncle. He swung himself up onto Starlight's back. "Come on, Johnnie. Let's go before we all grow old listening to advice."

Johnnie climbed onto Twinkleheels, and they set off, Starlight prancing and dancing in the lead, and Twinkleheels trotting steadily behind.

"He is a fool," Ebenezer murmured as he watched them go.

"Who?" asked a sparrow, who had landed on the fence rail. "The boy or the horse?"

"Does it matter?" Ebenezer said with a sigh. "They are two of a kind. I fear they will have to learn their lesson together."

The banks on both sides were steep and slick with dark, wet mud.

Twinkleheels stopped at the edge. He knew at once that this was no place to cross. He planted his feet firmly.

Starlight, however, came trotting right up to the edge and stopped short, snorting with alarm. He was used to clear water and clean bridges. This noisy, muddy water was a frightening new thing.

"Come on, Starlight, it's just a bit of water," Fred said, giving the horse a kick with his heels. "Get a move on!"

Starlight took one hesitant step forward, and his front hoof sank deep into the soft mud of the bank. He panicked. With a terrified squeal, he tried to pull back, but his struggles only made him sink deeper. He reared up, his eyes white with fear, and Fred, who was not expecting it, lost his balance and tumbled off into a soft patch of moss.

Fred was not hurt, but he was very angry. "Stupid horse!" he yelled, scrambling to his feet. "Now look what you've done!"

But Starlight was beyond listening. He was caught. His front legs were sunk to his chest in the thick, sucking mud, and the more he fought and thrashed, the more entangled he became in the low-hanging willow branches along the bank. He was trapped and terrified.

"Whoa, boy! Whoa!" Johnnie called, keeping Twinkleheels a safe distance away.

"Do something!" Fred shouted at Johnnie. "Don't just sit there!"

"I can't!" Johnnie said, his face pale. "He's stuck fast. And he's scared. If we get too close, he might hurt himself, or us!"

Starlight let out a pitiful, frightened whinny. It was not the sound of a proud champion. It was the sound of a very young, very scared horse who was in a great deal of trouble.

Johnnie looked at Fred, and then at the trapped horse, and then at the path back home. He knew what he had to do. "Stay with him, Fred," he said, his voice taking on a sudden firmness. "Try to keep him calm. Talk to him. Twinkleheels and I are going for help."

And before Fred could argue, Johnnie had turned Twinkleheels around and was urging him back up the path, towards the farm.

XX THE RESCUERS

Twinkleheels did not need to be urged. He knew the seriousness of the situation. He stretched his legs and settled into a steady, ground-eating canter. This was no race for show. This was a race against time, and against the fear that had gripped the proud horse Starlight.

Twinkleheels did not try to run his fastest. He had learned that lesson well. Instead, he ran his smartest. He picked his way sure-footedly along the path, avoiding the softest patches of mud and the slippery roots that crossed the trail. He kept his pace steady and strong, conserving his energy. For the first time, he was not thinking about himself at all. He was thinking only of the mission.

When they broke free of the woods, Johnnie let him have his head, and they flew across the greening fields. Old dog Spot saw them coming and began to bark, sensing that something was amiss.

"It's Starlight!" Johnnie gasped, sliding off Twinkleheels's back. "He's stuck! Down at the creek crossing. He's in the mud, up to his chest, and he can't get out!"

He looked up at the huge, gentle animals, and he was filled with a deep sense of awe. He remembered being stuck in the snowdrift, and how hopeless he had felt. And he knew, with absolute certainty, that these slow, steady creatures were exactly what was needed.

When they arrived at the creek, they found Fred sitting on a log, his face streaked with tears. Starlight was still trapped, and he had stopped struggling. He stood with his head hanging low, trembling and covered in mud. He looked like a very different horse from the proud champion who had left the barn that morning.

Farmer Green took charge at once. "All right, Fred, you stand well back," he said in a quiet, commanding voice. "Johnnie, hold Twinkleheels out of the way. Now, let's see what we have here."

He carefully approached the terrified horse, speaking to him in a low, soothing voice. "Easy now, fella. Easy does it. We'll have you out of there in a jiffy."

He worked calmly and efficiently, wrapping the wide canvas straps around Starlight's body, under his belly and behind his rump. He attached the straps to the long chains. Then he led the chains up the muddy bank to where Bright and Broad stood waiting as patiently as two stone statues.

"All right," Farmer Green said, checking the hitches one last time. He stood beside the oxen and laid a hand on Broad's flank. "Hup, boys," he said softly. "Easy now. Take it up. Hup!"

There was no sudden jerk. There was no great rush. The two oxen simply leaned forward, putting their immense weight into the yoke. Muscles bunched under their hides. The chains grew taut. For a moment, nothing seemed to happen. Then, with a great sucking, slopping sound, Starlight began to move. The oxen did not strain. They just pulled. It was a slow, steady, irresistible force, like a river's current or the turning of the earth.

Slowly, inch by inch, they drew the frightened horse up out of the mud and onto the solid ground of the path.

When he was free, Starlight stood shivering, covered from head to hoof in black mud, his beautiful coat ruined. He looked at the two great oxen who had saved him, and then he looked at the small pony, Twinkleheels, standing quietly with his boy. And for the first time, the proud show horse seemed to see them for what they were. He lowered his head in what looked very much like shame.

XXI A DIFFERENT KIND OF PRIDE

The walk back to the farm was a very quiet one. Fred walked beside his muddy, humbled horse, leading him by the halter. He did not say a word. Starlight, too, was silent, walking with his head low. Gone was all his prancing and dancing. He just plodded wearily along, like any common workhorse.

Farmer Green and Johnnie walked behind with the oxen and Twinkleheels.

"You see, Johnnie," Farmer Green said, "it's like I told you. Different work needs different tools. Starlight is a fine horse for a riding ring or a smooth road. But out here, where the going gets tough, you need strength and patience. You need Bright and Broad."

Johnnie nodded, looking at the two oxen with new eyes. "They saved him."

"They did," said Farmer Green. "And Twinkleheels here did his part. He was smart enough to know the danger, and fast enough to bring help. Everybody did the job they were suited for. That's how a farm works."

Twinkleheels heard this, and a feeling of warmth spread through him. It was a different kind of pride than he had ever felt before. It was not the proud feeling of being the fastest or the fanciest. It was the quiet, steady pride of being useful, of being part of a team.

Back in the barnyard, Farmer Green set about cleaning Starlight with buckets of warm water and brushes. Fred tried to help, but he seemed clumsy and unsure. Starlight stood perfectly still, letting them work. When they were finished, his slate-gray coat was clean again, but he did not seem to be the same horse. The arrogance was gone from his eyes.

Johnnie led Twinkleheels to his stall and gave him an extra measure of oats. "You were the real hero today, Twink," he whispered, scratching the pony behind the ears.

Later that evening, when the barn was quiet and filled with the soft sounds of horses munching their hay, Twinkleheels heard a small noise from the next stall. It was Starlight.

"Pony?" the show horse said, his voice very low.

"My name is Twinkleheels," the pony replied gently.

"Twinkleheels," Starlight repeated. "I... I was a fool today."

Twinkleheels was surprised. He had expected Starlight to remain silent and aloof. "We all do foolish things sometimes," he said, remembering his own race against Ebenezer.

"But I was cruel," Starlight went on. "I made fun of you, and of the old horse, and... and of the oxen. And they were the ones who saved me." He was quiet for a long moment. "I have never seen such strength. Not in a show ring. Not anywhere."

"They are strong," Twinkleheels agreed. "But they are gentle, too."

"I did not understand," Starlight murmured. "In the city, everything is about being the quickest, and the most elegant, and winning the blue ribbon. I thought that was all that mattered."

"It matters to be good at what you do," Twinkleheels said, echoing the words he had heard from Farmer Green and the lesson he had learned in his own heart. "But it also matters to know what you cannot do. And to be glad that others can."

Starlight was silent for so long that Twinkleheels thought he had nothing more to say. Then, the gray horse spoke again, his voice barely a whisper. "Thank you, Twinkleheels. For going for help."

"You are welcome," Twinkleheels said. He finished his oats and then, on an impulse, he pushed a few stray pieces of sweet clover from his manger through the bars of his stall, so they fell near Starlight's nose.

The show horse bent his elegant neck and ate the offering.

From the stall on the other side, old Ebenezer, who had been listening to the whole exchange, gave a soft, contented sigh. He knew that two hard lessons had been learned that day. And he knew that his young friend, the little pony with the quick feet and the now-wiser head, was growing up very well indeed. The barn was peaceful, and all was right with the world.

Farmer Green came out with Johnnie's Uncle Henry, and after a good deal of talk, it was decided that Starlight would stay in the stall next to Twinkleheels, a space that was usually empty. Johnnie led Twinkleheels into the barn, and Fred followed with Starlight.

The moment Starlight stepped onto the barn floor, he stopped again. "What is that peculiar smell?" he asked, wrinkling his nose.

"That's hay," Twinkleheels said quietly. "And molasses feed. And horses."

"Indeed," Starlight murmured. He looked at Ebenezer, who was dozing in the next stall. "My word. Is that old fellow still alive?"

Ebenezer opened one eye. "More alive than some that are half my age," he said in his low, rumbling voice. "And a good deal wiser, too."

Starlight simply gave a little, mocking whinny. The two bay horses, Lightfoot and High-step, who were always ready for some excitement, trotted to the front of their stalls to get a better look.

"My, what a handsome horse!" Lightfoot called out.

"Are you fast?" asked High-step.

"Faster than anything in this rustic place, I should imagine," Starlight replied, tossing his silky mane. He looked past Twinkleheels to the far end of the barn, where the broad backs of Bright and Broad were visible in their stalls. "And what, pray tell, are those enormous, lumbering beasts?"

"Those are Bright and Broad," Twinkleheels said, and there was a note of new respect in his voice. "They are oxen."

"Oxen!" Starlight laughed, a sound like ice clinking in a glass. "How positively medieval! I suppose you use them to drag stones about. At home, we have a tractor for such work."

Twinkleheels said no more. He lowered his head to his hay, but he found his appetite was not as good as it had been. He could feel Starlight's disdainful gaze upon him, and it was not a pleasant feeling.

"Pay him no mind," Ebenezer said softly from the next stall. "An empty bucket makes the loudest noise when you kick it."

Twinkleheels looked over at his old friend and felt a little better. But he knew that having Starlight on the farm was going to be a trial.

XVIII A FOOLISH CHALLENGE

The next morning, the sun shone brightly on a world that was turning from white to green. The last of the snow was melting quickly, leaving the ground soft and wet. After breakfast, Johnnie and his cousin Fred came out to the barn.

"Let's go for a ride!" Fred said eagerly. "I want to show you what Starlight can really do. A stuffy barn is no place for a champion."

"That's a great idea!" said Johnnie. "We can ride up to the old mill. The path along the creek is beautiful this time of year."

Fred looked at Twinkleheels, whom Johnnie was already starting to brush. "Are you going to ride... that?" he asked. "Starlight will be bored to tears, having to walk so slowly."

"Twinkleheels is plenty fast," Johnnie said defensively. "Aren't you, boy?" He gave Twinkleheels a pat, and the little pony nudged his shoulder.

"I have an idea," said Fred, a sly look in his eye. "Let's have a race! To the big willow tree at the bend in the creek and back. I'll even give you a head start."

Lightfoot and High-step, in the paddock, heard this and grew excited. "A race! A race!" they neighed to each other, kicking up their heels.

Starlight, being saddled by Fred, looked over at Twinkleheels with amusement. "Do you think your little legs can keep up, pony?" he sneered.

Twinkleheels looked at the soft, muddy ground of the barnyard. He looked at the wet fields beyond. He remembered the feeling of sinking, of struggling with no firm footing beneath him. And he remembered Farmer Green's words. "It takes oxen in such going."

"No," Twinkleheels said, so quietly that Johnnie had to lean in to hear him. "I don't want to race."

"What?" cried Fred. "Is he afraid?"

"He's not afraid!" Johnnie retorted. "He just doesn't want to." He looked at Twinkleheels with a puzzled expression. "Why not, Twink? You love to run."

Twinkleheels looked at his boy, and then at the proud Starlight, and then at the muddy ground. "The ground is too soft for racing," he said to Johnnie, trusting his boy to understand. "It is not safe."

Starlight let out a huff of contempt. "Nonsense! A little mud never hurt anyone. He's a coward, that's all. A timid little pony who is afraid to lose."

"He is not!" Johnnie's face was red with anger. "He beat Ebenezer in a race once! And Ebenezer is very wise!"

"He beat that old relic?" Starlight laughed again. "That proves nothing. I could beat him while trotting backwards. Very well, if the pony is too scared to race, we shall simply go for a ride. But do try to keep up, won't you?"

Farmer Green, who had come out to see the boys off, overheard the last of this. He walked over and ran a hand over Twinkleheels's neck. Then he looked at the ground, and up at the sky.

"The pony's right, boys," he said calmly. "The ground is treacherous today. It's slippery and soft. No day for racing. You just have a nice, slow ride, and be careful when you get to the creek. The banks will be slick as glass."

Fred looked annoyed, but he said nothing to his uncle. He swung himself up onto Starlight's back. "Come on, Johnnie. Let's go before we all grow old listening to advice."

Johnnie climbed onto Twinkleheels, and they set off, Starlight prancing and dancing in the lead, and Twinkleheels trotting steadily behind.

"He is a fool," Ebenezer murmured as he watched them go.

"Who?" asked a sparrow, who had landed on the fence rail. "The boy or the horse?"

"Does it matter?" Ebenezer said with a sigh. "They are two of a kind. I fear they will have to learn their lesson together."

XIX TROUBLE AT THE CREEK

The path wound away from the farm, through fields where the green shoots of spring were pushing through the earth. Starlight, with Fred on his back, did not seem to be able to walk in a straight line. He danced from one side of the path to the other, tossing his head and snatching at the bit. He was showing off.

"See how he moves!" Fred called back to Johnnie. "That's what a real show horse does. He has spirit!"

Twinkleheels just plodded along steadily. He felt the soft earth squish under his new shoes, and he placed his feet carefully. He knew this path. He knew where the ground was firm, and he knew where the winter frost had left it soft and boggy. He noticed that Starlight, for all his fancy stepping, did not seem to be paying any attention to the ground at all.

They soon came to the woods that bordered the creek. The air grew cooler under the shade of the tall pines and hemlocks. The path here was narrow, and the sound of rushing water grew louder.

"The creek's high!" Johnnie called out. "Father said it would be!"

They came to a place where the path dipped down to a crossing. It was not a bridge, but a place where the creek was usually shallow enough for a horse to walk through on a bed of smooth stones. But today was not a usual day. The melting snow from the hills had turned the gentle stream into a rushing, brown torrent. The water swirled and eddied, and the stony crossing was completely hidden. The banks on both sides were steep and slick with dark, wet mud.

Twinkleheels stopped at the edge. He knew at once that this was no place to cross. He planted his feet firmly.

Starlight, however, came trotting right up to the edge and stopped short, snorting with alarm. He was used to clear water and clean bridges. This noisy, muddy water was a frightening new thing.

"Come on, Starlight, it's just a bit of water," Fred said, giving the horse a kick with his heels. "Get a move on!"

Starlight took one hesitant step forward, and his front hoof sank deep into the soft mud of the bank. He panicked. With a terrified squeal, he tried to pull back, but his struggles only made him sink deeper. He reared up, his eyes white with fear, and Fred, who was not expecting it, lost his balance and tumbled off into a soft patch of moss.

Fred was not hurt, but he was very angry. "Stupid horse!" he yelled, scrambling to his feet. "Now look what you've done!"

But Starlight was beyond listening. He was caught. His front legs were sunk to his chest in the thick, sucking mud, and the more he fought and thrashed, the more entangled he became in the low-hanging willow branches along the bank. He was trapped and terrified.

"Whoa, boy! Whoa!" Johnnie called, keeping Twinkleheels a safe distance away.

"Do something!" Fred shouted at Johnnie. "Don't just sit there!"

"I can't!" Johnnie said, his face pale. "He's stuck fast. And he's scared. If we get too close, he might hurt himself, or us!"

Starlight let out a pitiful, frightened whinny. It was not the sound of a proud champion. It was the sound of a very young, very scared horse who was in a great deal of trouble.

Johnnie looked at Fred, and then at the trapped horse, and then at the path back home. He knew what he had to do. "Stay with him, Fred," he said, his voice taking on a sudden firmness. "Try to keep him calm. Talk to him. Twinkleheels and I are going for help."

And before Fred could argue, Johnnie had turned Twinkleheels around and was urging him back up the path, towards the farm.

XX THE RESCUERS

Twinkleheels did not need to be urged. He knew the seriousness of the situation. He stretched his legs and settled into a steady, ground-eating canter. This was no race for show. This was a race against time, and against the fear that had gripped the proud horse Starlight.

Twinkleheels did not try to run his fastest. He had learned that lesson well. Instead, he ran his smartest. He picked his way sure-footedly along the path, avoiding the softest patches of mud and the slippery roots that crossed the trail. He kept his pace steady and strong, conserving his energy. For the first time, he was not thinking about himself at all. He was thinking only of the mission.

When they broke free of the woods, Johnnie let him have his head, and they flew across the greening fields. Old dog Spot saw them coming and began to bark, sensing that something was amiss.

As they galloped into the barnyard, Farmer Green was just coming out of the workshop. He took one look at Johnnie's worried face and Twinkleheels's heaving sides.

"What is it, son? What's happened?"

"It's Starlight!" Johnnie gasped, sliding off Twinkleheels's back. "He's stuck! Down at the creek crossing. He's in the mud, up to his chest, and he can't get out!"

Farmer Green's face grew serious. He strode over and gave Twinkleheels a quick, approving pat. "You did well to come so fast, boy," he said to the pony. Then he turned his attention to the problem. He looked at the barn, and a calm, determined look came over his face.

"A horse in mud is a bad business," he said, more to himself than to Johnnie. "Panics them. A tractor would just tear up the bank and make it worse." He paused for a moment, thinking. "This is not a job for a horse. This is a job for Bright and Broad."

He went into the barn and came out a moment later with the heavy wooden yoke. "Johnnie," he commanded, "get the big chains from the shed. The ones with the canvas straps. And a coil of rope."

Twinkleheels watched as Farmer Green led the two great oxen from their stalls. They moved slowly, calmly, their large dark eyes blinking in the sunlight. They did not seem hurried or worried. They simply stood, patient and immense, as Farmer Green fitted the heavy yoke over their thick necks. There was a power in their stillness that was more impressive than all of Starlight's nervous prancing.

Johnnie came running back with the chains. Farmer Green looped them over Broad's yoke. "All right, son. Hop on Twinkleheels. You can show me the way."

The journey back to the creek was much slower. Bright and Broad moved with a deliberate, ponderous tread. Their huge, cloven hoofs spread out in the soft ground, giving them a firm footing where a horse would have slipped and slid. Twinkleheels, who was now rested, walked quietly beside them. He looked up at the huge, gentle animals, and he was filled with a deep sense of awe. He remembered being stuck in the snowdrift, and how hopeless he had felt. And he knew, with absolute certainty, that these slow, steady creatures were exactly what was needed.

When they arrived at the creek, they found Fred sitting on a log, his face streaked with tears. Starlight was still trapped, and he had stopped struggling. He stood with his head hanging low, trembling and covered in mud. He looked like a very different horse from the proud champion who had left the barn that morning.

Farmer Green took charge at once. "All right, Fred, you stand well back," he said in a quiet, commanding voice. "Johnnie, hold Twinkleheels out of the way. Now, let's see what we have here."

He carefully approached the terrified horse, speaking to him in a low, soothing voice. "Easy now, fella. Easy does it. We'll have you out of there in a jiffy."

He worked calmly and efficiently, wrapping the wide canvas straps around Starlight's body, under his belly and behind his rump. He attached the straps to the long chains. Then he led the chains up the muddy bank to where Bright and Broad stood waiting as patiently as two stone statues.

"All right," Farmer Green said, checking the hitches one last time. He stood beside the oxen and laid a hand on Broad's flank. "Hup, boys," he said softly. "Easy now. Take it up. Hup!"

There was no sudden jerk. There was no great rush. The two oxen simply leaned forward, putting their immense weight into the yoke. Muscles bunched under their hides. The chains grew taut. For a moment, nothing seemed to happen. Then, with a great sucking, slopping sound, Starlight began to move. The oxen did not strain. They just pulled. It was a slow, steady, irresistible force, like a river's current or the turning of the earth.

Slowly, inch by inch, they drew the frightened horse up out of the mud and onto the solid ground of the path.

When he was free, Starlight stood shivering, covered from head to hoof in black mud, his beautiful coat ruined. He looked at the two great oxen who had saved him, and then he looked at the small pony, Twinkleheels, standing quietly with his boy. And for the first time, the proud show horse seemed to see them for what they were. He lowered his head in what looked very much like shame.

XXI A DIFFERENT KIND OF PRIDE

The walk back to the farm was a very quiet one. Fred walked beside his muddy, humbled horse, leading him by the halter. He did not say a word. Starlight, too, was silent, walking with his head low. Gone was all his prancing and dancing. He just plodded wearily along, like any common workhorse.

Farmer Green and Johnnie walked behind with the oxen and Twinkleheels.

"You see, Johnnie," Farmer Green said, "it's like I told you. Different work needs different tools. Starlight is a fine horse for a riding ring or a smooth road. But out here, where the going gets tough, you need strength and patience. You need Bright and Broad."

Johnnie nodded, looking at the two oxen with new eyes. "They saved him."

"They did," said Farmer Green. "And Twinkleheels here did his part. He was smart enough to know the danger, and fast enough to bring help. Everybody did the job they were suited for. That's how a farm works."

Twinkleheels heard this, and a feeling of warmth spread through him. It was a different kind of pride than he had ever felt before. It was not the proud feeling of being the fastest or the fanciest. It was the quiet, steady pride of being useful, of being part of a team.

Back in the barnyard, Farmer Green set about cleaning Starlight with buckets of warm water and brushes. Fred tried to help, but he seemed clumsy and unsure. Starlight stood perfectly still, letting them work. When they were finished, his slate-gray coat was clean again, but he did not seem to be the same horse. The arrogance was gone from his eyes.

Johnnie led Twinkleheels to his stall and gave him an extra measure of oats. "You were the real hero today, Twink," he whispered, scratching the pony behind the ears.

Later that evening, when the barn was quiet and filled with the soft sounds of horses munching their hay, Twinkleheels heard a small noise from the next stall. It was Starlight.

"Pony?" the show horse said, his voice very low.

"My name is Twinkleheels," the pony replied gently.

"Twinkleheels," Starlight repeated. "I... I was a fool today."

Twinkleheels was surprised. He had expected Starlight to remain silent and aloof. "We all do foolish things sometimes," he said, remembering his own race against Ebenezer.

"But I was cruel," Starlight went on. "I made fun of you, and of the old horse, and... and of the oxen. And they were the ones who saved me." He was quiet for a long moment. "I have never seen such strength. Not in a show ring. Not anywhere."

"They are strong," Twinkleheels agreed. "But they are gentle, too."

"I did not understand," Starlight murmured. "In the city, everything is about being the quickest, and the most elegant, and winning the blue ribbon. I thought that was all that mattered."

"It matters to be good at what you do," Twinkleheels said, echoing the words he had heard from Farmer Green and the lesson he had learned in his own heart. "But it also matters to know what you cannot do. And to be glad that others can."

Starlight was silent for so long that Twinkleheels thought he had nothing more to say. Then, the gray horse spoke again, his voice barely a whisper. "Thank you, Twinkleheels. For going for help."

"You are welcome," Twinkleheels said. He finished his oats and then, on an impulse, he pushed a few stray pieces of sweet clover from his manger through the bars of his stall, so they fell near Starlight's nose.

The show horse bent his elegant neck and ate the offering.

From the stall on the other side, old Ebenezer, who had been listening to the whole exchange, gave a soft, contented sigh. He knew that two hard lessons had been learned that day. And he knew that his young friend, the little pony with the quick feet and the now-wiser head, was growing up very well indeed. The barn was peaceful, and all was right with the world.
